> **Source problems today:** the six Substack contestant/discovered feeds (Erik Torenberg, Gary Marcus, Dostoevsky's Blog, exponent, The Substack Post, Propel Earth) all 403'd again · Perplexity's research/ask/reason tools returned 403 "requires paid credits" on most digging lanes, perplexity_search still worked · NPR's Planet Money episode page and 99% Invisible's "Ship of Gold" transcript were unreachable from this machine · a Joe Rogan clip and a Radiolab episode surfaced material judged too politically live-wire to use and were dropped

> **Featured today**
>
> 1. **Officer ran past a beating and never saw it** · a restaged chase shows a majority of people miss a violent fight happening right next to them
> 2. **The Marlboro cowboy won a real elimination round** · the icon wasn't picked in the brainstorm, it won in the market against sea captains and weightlifters
> 3. **"No business being where they are"** · Qualcomm's CDMA bet was called a violation of the laws of physics before it became the basis of 3G
> 4. **Your face is hiding in your partner's face** · a 22% blend of your own face into your partner's photo is the version you find most attractive
> 5. **Investors called the name "too dumb to fund"** · Liquid Death's name and skull logo were rejected by every investor before becoming a $1.4B brand
> 6. **Heinz spent 8 years removing one tiny part** · a silicone valve was the only thing stopping 300 million ketchup caps a year from being recycled
> 7. **Spotify's founder deliberately hires doubt** · Daniel Ek says every team building something new needs a dedicated naysayer in the room

30 cards · Marketing 10 · Psychology 10 · Founders 10 · 8 wildcards

## Featured

### 1 · Officer ran past a beating and never saw it

**The find:** Boston officer Kenny Conley chased a suspect past a brutal assault on a fellow officer and swore under oath he never saw it — and was convicted of perjury for the claim. Researchers restaged the chase: volunteers ran after someone for three minutes past a staged fight 8 meters off the path. At night, only 35% noticed it; even in daylight, just 56% did.
**The surprise:** The study wasn't testing honesty, it was testing the physics of attention — and it found that missing a nearby fight while running a focused chase is the normal outcome, not a lie.
**The idea:** Inattentional blindness: focused pursuit narrows perception so completely that a violent, multi-person event in plain sight can go entirely unseen.

2 · Shocking number · Psychology · [i-Perception, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3485775/)

**In depth**

In January 1995, Boston police officer Kenny Conley chased a murder suspect through the streets of Roxbury after a shooting outside a nightclub on Blue Hill Avenue. Somewhere along that chase, a group of fellow officers — mistaking an undercover colleague, Michael Cox, for one of the fleeing suspects — beat Cox unconscious. Conley ran past the beating. When grand juries investigated the cover-up, Conley testified under oath that he hadn't seen it. Prosecutors didn't believe him: he was indicted in 1997, convicted in 2000 of perjury and obstruction of justice, and sentenced to 34 months in prison. The case became a symbol of police "blue wall of silence" culture — a cop supposedly lying to protect his own. His conviction was eventually thrown out (a federal judge ruled he hadn't gotten a fair trial, and in 2011 the government dropped the case rather than retry him), and a separate civil jury also cleared him. He later rejoined the Boston Police Department and, in recent years, holds rank as a sergeant detective.

In 2011, Harvard psychologist Christopher Chabris, with Adam Weinberger, Matthew Fontaine, and Daniel Simons, published "You Do Not Talk About Fight Club if You Do Not Notice Fight Club" in the journal i-Perception to test whether Conley's claim was psychologically plausible rather than a lie. They had participants run after a confederate for about three minutes along a real campus path, replicating the chase. Along the route, a staged fight — three confederates — broke out roughly 8 meters off the path. Running the test at night, only 35% of participants noticed the fight; in daylight, 56% noticed. Adding a dual cognitive task (tracking two separate counts, mimicking an officer's divided attention while pursuing a suspect) further reduced noticing. In the condition closest to Conley's actual circumstances — nighttime, under cognitive load, while chasing someone — a majority of ordinary people missed an ongoing assault happening in plain sight just off their path.

This sits in the same research lineage as Simons and Chabris's famous 1999 "invisible gorilla" experiment, where observers asked to count basketball passes in a video missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Both studies demonstrate inattentional blindness: people routinely fail to perceive fully visible objects or events when their attention is focused elsewhere, even at full alertness. The Conley study extended that lab finding into a real-world, high-stakes forensic application — directly challenging the legal and juror assumption that "if it happened in front of you, you must have seen it," with implications for how courts weigh eyewitness and bystander testimony.

Further links: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23145232/ · https://news.illinois.edu/study-suggests-police-officer-wrongfully-convicted-for-missing-the-obvious/ · https://www.npr.org/2011/06/20/137086464/why-seeing-the-unexpected-is-often-not-believing · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cox_(police_officer)

### 2 · The Marlboro cowboy won a real elimination round

**The find:** In December 1954, Leo Burnett's team brainstormed how to relaunch Marlboro as a masculine cigarette. The room threw out cab driver, sailor, marine, pilot and race car driver before someone said "cowboy," and the table agreed instantly. Philip Morris nearly killed it — research found only about 3,000 full-time cowboys in the whole US — but the ad ran anyway, alongside sea captains, weightlifters and war correspondents as a rotating cast of "masculine" figures.
**The surprise:** The enduring icon wasn't chosen by elimination in the pitch meeting. It was one guess among several that all ran in parallel for years, and the market, not the room, picked the winner.
**The idea:** Reframing: a single enduring icon often starts as one of several ideas run side by side; the real elimination happens in public, not in the brainstorm.

1 · Hidden reason · Marketing · [Marlboro Man history](http://wesclark.com/temp/marlboro.html)

**In depth**

In December 1954, on a Saturday before Christmas, Leo Burnett invited his creative staff out to his farm south of Chicago to solve a specific problem: Philip Morris's Marlboro, a filtered cigarette sold since 1924 as a women's brand with the slogan "Mild as May" and a red "beauty tip" designed to hide lipstick stains, held well under 1% of the US cigarette market and needed to relaunch as a man's cigarette alongside a new flip-top box. Burnett asked the room a simple question: "What is the most masculine figure in America?" The answers came fast — cab driver, sailor, marine, pilot, race car driver — and then someone said "cowboy," and the table agreed almost instantly. Copywriter Draper Daniels supplied the line that would run under the first ad: "Delivers the goods on flavor." Burnett already had an image in mind: a 1949 Life magazine photo essay by Leonard McCombe on Clarence Hailey "C.H." Long, a 39-year-old foreman on the 320,000-acre JA Ranch in the Texas panhandle. The idea nearly died before it launched — Philip Morris commissioned research that found only about 3,000 full-time working cowboys existed in the entire United States, and executives questioned how office workers in Manhattan were supposed to relate to one. Burnett argued his way past the objection, and the cowboy ad ran in January 1955, making Marlboro the top-selling cigarette in greater New York within 30 days.

The cowboy was never meant to be the whole campaign — just the opening entry in a planned rotation of "masculine confidence" types: sea captains, weightlifters, war correspondents, construction workers, sailors, pilots, scientists, farmers, and tattooed regular guys, several played by agency and Philip Morris staff themselves. That mixed cast ran through the mid-to-late 1950s under the jingle "You get a lot to like — filter, flavor, flip-top box." But the numbers separated the cowboy from the pack: Marlboro sold roughly 18 million cigarettes in 1954, then 6.4-6.7 billion in 1955, 14.3 billion in 1956, and 19.5 billion in 1957 — about three times as many cigarettes in a single day as in all of 1954. By 1958, with 4.5% US market share, the tattooed-men and other non-cowboy figures were quietly dropped, and Burnett's team concentrated entirely on cowboys — later, after 1963, actual working cowboys and rodeo riders set to Elmer Bernstein's "Magnificent Seven" theme. Market share climbed through the following decades: roughly 10% by 1970, the #1-selling US brand by 1972, and around 40% of the US market by 2017 — the longest-running and most successful brand mascot in advertising history, run until 1999.

Further links: http://wesclark.com/temp/marlboro.html · https://adage.com/article/news/viewpoint-annals-advertising/93163/ · https://quartr.com/insights/edge/making-the-marlboro-man · https://tobacco-img.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/06212327/marlboro_oralhistory.pdf

### 3 · "No business being where they are"

**The find:** In the early 1990s, the US cellular industry had already picked a rival standard (TDMA) over Qualcomm's CDMA technology, a Stanford professor said CDMA "violated the laws of physics," and the San Diego Union-Tribune's own coverage said bluntly that Qualcomm "have no business being where they are." Qualcomm's Irwin Jacobs kept building CDMA anyway. It became the technical foundation of 3G, and is in most smartphones today.
**The surprise:** The press didn't just doubt the bet — in print, they said the company had no business existing, after the industry had already voted against its technology.
**The idea:** Right idea, wrong time: when a technical "law" everyone cites turns out to be an engineering assumption, not a physical constant, outlasting the consensus can be the whole strategy.

3 · Wrong decision that worked · Founders · [San Diego Union-Tribune](https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2018/03/18/flurry-of-activity-around-qualcomm-highlights-companys-history-of-defying-expectations/)

**In depth**

Irwin Jacobs earned a doctorate from MIT, taught electrical engineering there and then at UC San Diego, and in 1968 co-founded Linkabit with Andrew Viterbi, building satellite and encryption systems that grew to 1,400-plus employees before a 1980 sale to M/A-COM. Jacobs left three years later and, on July 1, 1985, launched Qualcomm with six co-founders, each putting in roughly $1,500. By the late 1980s the US cellular industry had a problem: analog networks were running out of capacity, and in 1989 the CTIA's member carriers and manufacturers — AT&T, Motorola, Ericsson, Nortel — picked TDMA, standardized as IS-54, as the digital upgrade path, largely because it was closest to ready. Qualcomm, pitching a different scheme called CDMA (adapted from military spread-spectrum communications, where every call is spread across the whole frequency band simultaneously rather than sliced into time slots), was treated as a late, implausible entrant. Stanford electrical engineering professor Bruce Lusignan became CDMA's most vocal academic critic, arguing in forums and later in a 1996 LA Times piece that the scheme lacked adequate protection from signal fading and couldn't deliver the capacity gains Qualcomm claimed. Writer George Gilder later popularized the sharper framing that the objection amounted to saying CDMA "violated the laws of physics." A Wall Street Journal piece in 1996 argued Jacobs's promotion was pushing carriers to waste billions on unproven technology.

Jacobs kept building: a pivotal November 1989 demo for over 100 executives nearly collapsed when a GPS timing glitch hit the base stations, but the team recovered during a 45-minute scramble and the system worked. The TIA approved CDMA as IS-95 in July 1993. Verizon's predecessors and Sprint bet on CDMA while AT&T stuck with TDMA/GSM-style paths; South Korea's government adopted CDMA nationally in 1993 and launched the world's first commercial CDMA network on January 1, 1996, hitting over a million subscribers within the year — proof-of-scale that preceded the US rollout. Europe's GSM camp fought Qualcomm's IP during 3G standardization; Ericsson and Qualcomm settled a two-and-a-half-year patent dispute in March 1999, cross-licensing CDMA, WCDMA and cdma2000 patents and clearing the ITU's path to a WCDMA 3G standard built on Qualcomm's patented core. Qualcomm's stock then became the single best performer in the S&P 500 for 1999, up roughly 2,600%. The company's licensing arm now collects royalties on virtually every 3G/4G/5G phone sold regardless of chip supplier, generating billions annually at operating margins often above 60-70%, long after the "laws of physics" objection evaporated.

Further links: https://spectrum.ieee.org/irwin-jacobs-captain-of-cdma · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualcomm · https://money.cnn.com/1999/03/25/europe/ericsson/ · https://sandiegohistory.org/journal/v55-1/pdf/v55-1west.pdf

### 4 · Your face is hiding in your partner's face

**The find:** Researchers digitally blended a small slice of each subject's own face into a photo of their real-life partner. The blend rated most attractive wasn't 0% or 33% — it centered on 22% self-resemblance, beating a version blended with an independently-rated "ideal" face. Subjects never consciously detected their own face in the photo.
**The surprise:** People unknowingly find their partner most attractive when the partner's face carries a little of their own in it, and they can't tell why or that it's happening.
**The idea:** Mere exposure effect: we're implicitly drawn to a narrow, unconscious sweet spot of self-similarity, not to maximum objective beauty.

2 · Shocking number · Psychology · [Laeng et al., PLOS ONE 2013](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0068395)

**In depth**

In 2013, University of Oslo psychologist Bruno Laeng, with Oddrun Vermeer and Unni Sulutvedt, published "Is Beauty in the Face of the Beholder?" in PLOS ONE. They recruited 20 heterosexual couples (40 people, average age 28, together at least two years), photographed each partner, and used morphing software to blend small percentages of one partner's own face into a photo of their real-life partner, altering only the internal features (eyes, nose, mouth region) so the base face stayed clearly recognizable. Each participant then ranked seven morphed versions of their partner's face: a 22% self-blend, blends with an average male or female "prototype" face, a blend with an androgynous prototype, blends with independently-rated "best" composite faces, and a mirror-symmetry version. Across both male and female participants, the 22% self-blend was ranked most attractive, beating the prototype and "best face" morphs by wide margins. A control group of unrelated raters, shown the same images with no personal stake, ranked those same self-blended photos dead last — confirming the effect depended on the viewer's own face being secretly present, not on some neutral quality of the blend.

A second experiment tested three resemblance doses (11%, 22%, 33%) on 10 of the couples: 22% again won; 11% and 33% dropped to the bottom, suggesting a specific sweet spot rather than "more is better." A third experiment used a forced-choice detection task and found participants performed no better than chance at noticing their own face had been blended in — the preference operated entirely unconsciously. The researchers framed this as evidence for "positive assortative mating": people are implicitly drawn to phenotypic self-similarity in mates, a pull theorized to run through imprinting-like, mere-exposure, and kin-recognition mechanisms, but kept in check by an opposing pressure to avoid incest-like pairings, producing a moderate rather than maximal resemblance optimum. The same lab followed up in 2014 by blending participants' own faces versus their opposite-sex parent's face into attractiveness-rated composites, finding the self-based standard dominated over a parental-imprinting standard. A 2016 study found the self-resemblance preference appeared mainly in partnered people, not singles, who instead preferred dissimilar faces. Separately, real-world assortative-mating research has repeatedly shown raters can match real spouses' photos to each other above chance, indicating actual couples resemble each other facially more than random pairings, independent of any "growing to look alike" over time.

Further links: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0068395 · https://peerj.com/articles/595/ · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4906020/ · https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0191456

### 5 · Investors called the name "too dumb to fund"

**The find:** When Mike Cessario pitched canned water branded "Liquid Death" with a melting skull logo, beverage-industry contacts and investors said the cans "looked too much like beer" and that no retailer would stock something that says "Death" on it. He self-funded a $1,500 mock commercial instead; it hit about 3 million views and nearly 80,000 Facebook followers before a single can existed. By 2022 the company was doing around $130 million in sales at a $700 million valuation.
**The surprise:** The exact name and look that investors said would keep the product off shelves is now sold in tens of thousands of stores, including Kroger and Target.
**The idea:** Anti-branding: when a category is commoditized and attention is the real bottleneck, a name that "shouldn't work" can function as free distribution.

3 · Wrong decision that worked · Marketing · [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2022/11/26/liquid-death-ceo-mike-cessario-we-chose-the-dumbest-possible-name-for-water.html)

**In depth**

Mike Cessario spent roughly a decade as an advertising creative director before founding Liquid Death — working at agencies including Crispin Porter + Bogusky and VaynerMedia, then as a creative director at Netflix, where he led marketing campaigns for "Stranger Things," "Narcos," and "House of Cards," plus viral work for Toyota and Mountain Dew. The idea traces to 2009, when he watched musicians at the Vans Warped Tour in Denver drinking water out of Monster Energy cans to stay hydrated without looking uncool onstage — he wondered why only beer and energy drinks got to look dangerous and fun while water was stuck looking clinical. He filed the "Liquid Death" trademark in July 2017 with a melting-skull logo on a tallboy can styled like a craft beer. When he shopped the concept to beverage-industry contacts and investors, the universal response was rejection: the cans "looked too much like beer" and would confuse shoppers, and retailers would never put something on a shelf that said "Death" on it. No investor would write a check for the concept alone.

So in 2018, with no product and no funding, Cessario took a 3D rendering of the can and shot a two-minute mock commercial for about $1,500, then spent a few thousand more in paid media behind it. Over roughly four to five months it reached about 3 million views and nearly 80,000 Facebook followers — more than Aquafina's entire Facebook following at the time — with hundreds of comments asking where to buy it, even though the can didn't exist yet. That traction became the pitch deck. In January 2019, Science Inc. led a $1.6 million seed round (investors included Twitter's Biz Stone and Away's Jen Rubio), and Liquid Death began selling direct-to-consumer that month. Growth then compounded through funding rounds: $9 million (2020), $23 million (2020), $75 million at a $525 million valuation (January 2022), $70 million at $700 million (October 2022), and $67 million at $1.4 billion (March 2024). Revenue went from about $10 million (2020) to roughly $130 million (2022) to about $333 million (2024), with distribution expanding from Whole Foods to 7-Eleven, Publix, Kroger, and Target. The clean growth story hides a real near-collapse: Liquid Death initially canned product in Austria and shipped it to the US, and when COVID-era ocean freight costs spiked, the company was losing money on every case sold — the faster it grew, the more it lost — forcing it to fix sourcing and logistics. The company has never reported a profitable year, underscoring that canned water is a heavy, low-margin product where freight and aluminum costs eat most of the markup regardless of how hot the brand is.

Further links: https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2022/11/26/liquid-death-ceo-mike-cessario-we-chose-the-dumbest-possible-name-for-water.html · https://www.cnbc.com/2019/05/07/ex-netflix-creative-director-raises-1point6-million-for-liquid-death-canned-water.html · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Death · https://sacra.com/c/liquid-death/

### 6 · Heinz spent 8 years removing one tiny part

**The find:** Heinz's flip-top ketchup cap used a tiny silicone valve for decades to control flow and stop drips. Heinz's own patent states that caps "lacking a silicon membrane" are "more easily recyclable," because silicone can't be mechanically separated from the plastic shell at recycling scale. Replacing the valve with pure internal channel geometry — exploiting ketchup's own thinning-under-pressure behavior — took eight years, 45 prototypes, 185,000 engineering hours and $1.2 million, eliminating roughly 300 million unrecyclable caps a year.
**The surprise:** The hardest, most expensive engineering problem wasn't making the cap work — it already worked — it was making it work with one fewer material.
**The idea:** Logistics-driven design: the biggest hidden cost of a well-functioning design can be a tiny secondary material nobody notices, and removing it, not improving it, is sometimes the whole challenge.

1 · Hidden reason · Marketing · [Lumafield](https://www.lumafield.com/first-article/posts/heinzs-sustainable-ketchup-cap)

**In depth**

For decades, every Heinz squeeze bottle cap concealed a trick: a tiny silicone valve, molded into a polypropylene flip-top shell, that flexed open under squeeze pressure and sealed itself shut the instant you let go — the mechanism behind the "perfect squeeze" and the clean stop. That same silicone speck was also why the cap was trash. Silicone and polypropylene can't be mechanically separated at the scale and speed recycling facilities operate at, and the United States has, by most counts, effectively one plant that recycles silicone. So for years, roughly 300 million Heinz caps went to landfill annually even as the PET bottles around them got recycled. Heinz's own utility patent, US 12,686,535 B2 ("Container, closure, and methods for manufacture," filed January 2023, assigned to H.J. Heinz Company Brands LLC), states the problem plainly: the closure "may be formed with or without a silicon membrane or rubber valve," and "if the closure cap lacks a silicon membrane, the closure cap may be more easily recyclable."

Heinz and manufacturing partner Berry Global spent eight to nine years and, per Kraft Heinz's own figures, 45 prototypes, more than 185,000 engineering hours, and $1.2 million solving it — not by finding a recyclable substitute material, but by eliminating the second material altogether. The new cap is pure polypropylene, and it replaces the valve's job with pure geometry: an internal antechamber and a maze of channels that force ketchup along an indirect path before it reaches the nozzle. Ketchup is shear-thinning — it stays thick at rest but thins and flows under strain — so a firm squeeze pushes it through the constricted channels where it loosens and dispenses at a controlled rate, while at rest its regained viscosity plus the indirect path keeps it from dripping, no elastic membrane required. CT scans by the engineering firm Lumafield visually confirmed the shift: the old cap shows up as two distinct-density materials, the new one as a single uniform mass. Kraft Heinz senior packaging sustainability manager Trenten Huntington noted the team "tested over 45 prototypes to find the optimal solution that balances functionality, ease of use, and aesthetics." The cap launched in the UK on Heinz Tomato Ketchup bottles in mid-to-late 2023, expanded across more Heinz sauces in the UK and Europe through 2024-2025, and as of this writing has not been confirmed for a US rollout — meaning the fix for an American recycling gap debuted everywhere except America.

Further links: https://www.lumafield.com/first-article/posts/heinzs-sustainable-ketchup-cap · https://patents.google.com/patent/US12686535B2/en · https://news.kraftheinzcompany.com/press-releases-details/2021/Heinz-Tomato-Ketchup-Introduces-First-100-Recyclable-Cap-Delivering-the-Perfect-Eco-Friendly-Squeeze/default.aspx · https://www.thecooldown.com/green-business/kraft-heinz-uk-ketchup-bottle-recyclable-lid/

### 7 · Spotify's founder deliberately hires doubt

**The find:** Daniel Ek, the co-founder and CEO who grew Spotify from a Swedish startup into a $100-billion-plus streaming company, says every team building something new deliberately needs a dedicated contrarian: "You need the naysayer in the room as well. You need the people who will balance it out and be the one who says, 'I'm not sure this is going to work out.'"
**The surprise:** Founder culture usually prizes unbroken conviction and surrounding yourself with believers. One of the most successful founders alive says the opposite — hire for doubt on purpose.
**The idea:** Founder mode: conviction without an institutionalized skeptic isn't boldness, it's an unchecked blind spot — dissent is a feature of the team, not a threat to morale.

8 · Unexpected claim · Founders · [The Diary of a CEO, at 00:10:33](https://podcasts.happyscribe.com/the-diary-of-a-ceo-with-steven-bartlett/most-replayed-moment-the-one-habit-behind-every-breakthrough-idea-spotify-founder-08887453-954a-4240-9e52-f9495145df1e)

**In depth**

Daniel Ek co-founded Spotify with Martin Lorentzon in 2006 in Stockholm, a scrappy startup born out of Ek's frustration with music piracy. Ek, born 1983, had already built and sold an online ad company (Advertigo, sold to Tradedoubler in 2006) and briefly run µTorrent before turning to music. He has said, including on this podcast, that he initially thought a legal streaming service was a "terrible idea" given how entrenched piracy was — the breakthrough reframe was to stop trying to legislate piracy away and instead build something that simply worked better than stealing music. Spotify launched in October 2008 after two years of licensing negotiations with major labels. As of late 2026, Spotify has roughly 300 million paying Premium subscribers and 777-800 million total monthly active users, trailing-twelve-month revenue near $22 billion, and a market capitalization clustering between about $122 billion and $129 billion — up from an early-2010s valuation in the single-digit billions. Ek stepped down as CEO at the end of 2025, remaining executive chairman; his net worth was estimated at roughly $12.5 billion in August 2026.

The naysayer quote comes from a "Most Replayed Moment" clip (published November 6, 2026, recorded October 29, 2026) pulled from Ek's full-length Diary of a CEO interview with Steven Bartlett. At roughly 00:10:33, discussing the habit behind breakthrough ideas, Ek says: "You need the naysayer in the room as well. You need the people who will balance it out and be the one who says, 'I'm not sure this is going to work out.'" The surrounding context is Bartlett probing the shared optimism between Ek and Lorentzon during Spotify's hardest early years. Ek pushes back on the idea that optimism alone explains the company's survival — he argues unchecked optimism breeds groupthink, and that contrarian voices are what keep a founding team honest. He frames it as role-specific: a CFO should be the skeptic questioning the sales pipeline, a salesperson should be the believer pushing forward, and a healthy team deliberately mixes both rather than hiring only true believers. This echoes, but is not identical to, Amazon's "disagree and commit" principle, where dissent is encouraged before a decision but full buy-in is expected after — Ek's version is about permanently embedding a dissenting voice in the room rather than resolving disagreement once and moving on.

Further links: https://podcasts.happyscribe.com/the-diary-of-a-ceo-with-steven-bartlett/most-replayed-moment-the-one-habit-behind-every-breakthrough-idea-spotify-founder-08887453-954a-4240-9e52-f9495145df1e · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ek · https://fortune.com/europe/2023/09/28/spotify-ceo-daniel-ek-platform-terrible-idea-lost-hair-gained-30lbs-success · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disagree_and_commit

## The rest

### 8 · Crosswalk buttons that do nothing

**The find:** In most dense US downtowns, most pedestrian crosswalk buttons are disconnected. Pressing one does nothing — the lights run on a fixed timed cycle built for traffic flow, not for anyone pressing a button.
**The surprise:** Cities never removed the dead buttons. Keeping a control that changes nothing still measurably calms impatient pedestrians and makes the wait feel less pointless.
**The idea:** Illusion of control: a visible, costless action gives people a sense of influence over an outcome they can't actually change, and that feeling alone makes waiting easier.

1 · Hidden reason · Marketing · [Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2017/07/24/ahead-and-press-that-pedestrian-button-makes-you-feel-good/1krGOm2CfeZBvIkEkNm5rL/story.html)

### 9 · A bonus teachers could lose doubled scores

**The find:** In a Chicago Heights field experiment, one group of teachers got a standard bonus at year-end tied to their students' gains. Another group got the same expected bonus paid up front, with a contract to return part of it if students underperformed. The "give it back" framing raised math scores by 0.2 to 0.4 standard deviations; the standard year-end bonus produced no measurable effect at all.
**The surprise:** The money on offer was identical. Only the framing changed — earn it later vs. keep it now, only if you deliver — and that framing alone outperformed most tested education interventions.
**The idea:** Loss aversion doesn't need a gamble or a lab choice to work; paying people first and threatening to take money back drives more effort than offering the same money as a future reward.

2 · Shocking number · Psychology · [NBER Working Paper 18237](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w18237/w18237.pdf)

### 10 · Netflix's "right" countdown was a guess

**The find:** The engineer who built Netflix's "next episode" autoplay says the team tested 5, 10 and 15-second countdowns before shipping. Ten seconds produced the biggest lift in hours watched of any feature they'd tested at the time.
**The surprise:** The team's own explanation was that 10 seconds "felt right." Netflix later cut it to 5 seconds and watch time rose again, so the "digestion time" story wasn't the real driver.
**The idea:** Default effect: flipping the decision from "choose to continue" to "choose to stop" does almost all the work; the exact timer is secondary, and the reason given for it afterward is often just a story.

1 · Hidden reason · Founders · wildcard · [Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=20566514)

### 11 · A $199,000 house sells for more

**The find:** A study of more than 370,000 Virginia home listings found that "just below" pricing — $199,000 instead of $200,000 — let sellers set a higher starting ask without scaring off buyers. Those homes closed 2.5-3% higher than identical homes listed at the round number.
**The surprise:** It's the same house either way. The single leftmost digit on the listing moved the final sale price by thousands of dollars, even though the round-priced homes sold faster.
**The idea:** Anchoring at work on the biggest single purchase most people ever make: the first number a buyer sees recalibrates what the whole house feels worth, before anyone has seen a room.

2 · Shocking number · Marketing · [Journal of Housing Research](https://doi.org/10.1080/10835547.2015.12092101)

### 12 · A photo of eyes made gym-goers wipe down

### 13 · One order forced In-N-Out's burger cap

**The find:** Until 2004, In-N-Out would build a burger of any size a customer asked for. ### 14 · Naming the hours beat naming the benefit

### 15 · One sign closed the handwashing gap

### 18 · An airport made the walk to bags longer

### 19 · LEGO's own sons fought the plastic brick

### 26 · The milk carton was a self-refreshing billboard

### 30 · Pianos are tuned to be equally wrong

**The find:** A piano can't be tuned so every interval is mathematically pure — the math doesn't close. So tuners settled on "equal temperament": spreading the unavoidable error evenly across all twelve notes, so every key is equally, imperceptibly out of tune rather than some keys pure and others unplayable.
**The surprise:** The instrument millions of people think of as "in tune" is, by design, uniformly mistuned. Perfection in any one key was sacrificed on purpose so the whole system would work.
**The idea:** Cross-domain transfer: when a perfect fit is mathematically impossible, deliberately spreading the imperfection evenly often beats optimizing one part at the expense of the rest.
